q: Which set of Python keywords lets a program perform different actions depending on a Boolean condition?
options: switch, case, default
when, otherwise, unless
if, elif, else
try, except, finally
explanation: Conditional expressions in Python are built from if, elif, and else. switch/case/default is the style of other languages, when/otherwise/unless are not Python keywords, and try/except/finally handles errors rather than Boolean decisions.

q: How many distinct values can a Python Boolean take?
options: Two: True and False
Three: True, False, and None
Two: the integers 1 and 0 only
Any integer, because every nonzero integer counts as a Boolean value
explanation: A Boolean is exactly one of two values, True or False. None is a separate value, not a Boolean. Integers can be treated as True or False inside a condition, but that does not make every integer a Boolean value.

q: What does print(10 != 10) output?
options: True, because != tests whether two values are the same and 10 is the same as 10
Nothing, because a comparison alone cannot be printed
An error, because != is not a valid Python operator
False, because the two values are equal so the not-equal test fails
explanation: != is the not-equal operator and is True only when the values differ. Since 10 equals 10, the result is False. The first option confuses != with ==, and comparisons can be printed like any other expression.

q: Given test = True, what does print(not test) output?
options: None, because not removes the value from the variable
False
An error, because not can only be applied to comparison expressions
True, because not leaves a Boolean variable unchanged
explanation: not negates or reverses a Boolean value, so not True is False. It does not delete the value, it works on Boolean variables as well as comparisons, and it does not leave the value unchanged.

q: The and operator is used to judge whether:
options: all arguments in a set are True
at least one argument in a set is True
exactly one argument in a set is True
no argument in a set is True
explanation: and requires all arguments to be True. At least one describes or. Exactly one and none are not what either operator tests.

q: If x = True and y = False, what are the results of (x and y) and (x or y), in that order?
options: True and True
False and False
False and True
True and False
explanation: x and y needs both True, so it is False. x or y needs at least one True, so it is True. The result is False then True.

q: Under which circumstance does x or y evaluate to False when x and y are Booleans?
options: When at least one of x and y is True
When exactly one of x and y is False
When only the first value is True
When both x and y are False
explanation: or is False only when every operand is False. If at least one operand is True (including the case where only the first is True), the result is True.

q: x = 3 and y = 5. What is the value of z in z = x and y?
options: 3, because the first argument is returned whenever both are nonzero
5, the second argument
True, because both values are nonzero
8, because and combines two nonzero values by adding them
explanation: With numbers, and returns the second argument when both are True (nonzero). Both 3 and 5 are nonzero, so z = 5. and does not return a Boolean here and never adds values.

q: x = 4 and y = 0. What is the value of z in z = x and y?
options: 4, because the first argument is always returned by and
True, because x is nonzero and so the whole expression is True
0, the first False argument
False, because and always returns a Boolean value
explanation: When one argument is False (0), and evaluates to the first False argument, which is y = 0. It does not always return the first argument, and with numbers it returns an operand rather than a Boolean.

q: x = 0 and y = 9. What is the value of z in z = x or y?
options: 9, the first True argument
0, because or returns the first argument that it examines
True, because or always produces a Boolean result
None, because the two arguments disagree in truth value
explanation: With numbers, or evaluates to the first True argument when at least one argument is True. x = 0 is False, y = 9 is True, so z = 9. It does not return None and does not convert the result to a Boolean.

q: x = "" (an empty string) and y = 0. What is the value of z in z = x or y?
options: The empty string, because x is the first argument and is returned
0, the second argument
False, because both values are False-like and or returns a Boolean
An error, because a string and an integer cannot be combined with or
explanation: When both arguments are False, or evaluates to the second argument, so z = 0. Mixed types are allowed, and or does not convert the result to a Boolean.

q: What does an IF statement do with its body?
options: It repeats the body until the condition becomes False
It runs the body once and then evaluates the condition to check the result
It chooses the body by matching the condition against a list of values
It executes the body only when the condition evaluates to True
explanation: IF evaluates the Boolean expression first and runs the body only when it is True, otherwise the body is skipped. Repeating is the job of loops, the condition is evaluated before the body, and matching against values describes match case.

q: Which line shows valid IF statement syntax in Python?
options: if condition: followed by an indented body
if (condition) { body } using curly braces around the body
if condition then body end if with a closing keyword
if condition; body; with a semicolon after the condition
explanation: Python writes if condition: with a colon and an indented body. Curly braces, then/end if, and semicolons belong to other languages.

q: Given n = 0, what is printed by the statement if n: print("yes") else: print("no")?
options: yes, because n has been assigned a value
Nothing, because 0 is not a valid condition
no
An error, because an integer cannot be used as a condition
explanation: Any integer is treated as True except 0, which is treated as False. So the IF body is skipped and the ELSE body prints no. Integers are valid conditions.

q: Which string value is treated as False when used as an IF condition?
options: "False" (the word False)
"" (the empty string)
" " (a string holding one space)
"0" (a string holding the digit zero)
explanation: Only the empty string is treated as False. Any string that has a value, including the word False, a single space, or the character 0, is treated as True.

q: When is the condition of an ELIF clause evaluated?
options: Every time the program runs, independently of the IF statement before it
Only after the IF condition has evaluated to True, as a follow-up check
Only when the program has no ELSE clause available to handle the case
Only if the earlier conditions in the chain were evaluated as False
explanation: ELIF checks additional conditions only if the first condition (usually the IF) is False. If the IF is True the ELIF is skipped, and the presence of an ELSE has no effect on this.

q: a = 5 and b = 5. What is printed by: if b > a: print("b is greater than a") elif a == b: print("a and b are equal")?
options: a and b are equal
b is greater than a
Both messages are printed
Nothing is printed
explanation: b > a is False (5 is not greater than 5), so the ELIF is checked. a == b is True, so only the second message prints.

q: Why is an if/elif chain generally preferred over several separate IF statements for mutually exclusive cases?
options: Separate IF statements are a syntax error when they test related conditions
elif branches run faster because Python compiles them into a lookup table instead of tests
elif branches are skipped once an earlier condition in the chain was True
Separate IF statements cannot use Boolean expressions as conditions
explanation: ELIF statements do not execute if an earlier IF is already True, so only one branch runs. Separate IF statements are legal but generally not recommended. The speed and syntax-error claims are false, and IF accepts any Boolean expression.

q: An ELSE clause executes its body when:
options: The IF condition is True
Any one of the preceding conditions evaluates to False
Execution reaches it, regardless of how the earlier conditions evaluated
All preceding conditional statements evaluate to False
explanation: ELSE runs only if every preceding condition is False. Running when the IF is True is the opposite. One False condition is not enough, since another earlier branch may have been True. Reaching it does not guarantee execution.

q: Where does an ELSE clause normally appear in a conditional chain?
options: First, before the IF statement
Between the IF statement and the first ELIF
Last, after the IF and any ELIF statements
Anywhere, because its position does not affect program behavior
explanation: ELSE is usually the last statement after IF and ELIF, because it handles whatever none of the previous conditions caught.

q: What is a nested IF-ELSE statement?
options: An IF or ELIF statement placed inside another IF or ELIF block
Several independent IF statements written one after another at the same level
An ELSE statement written without any preceding IF
A chain of ELIF statements that ends with a default ELSE clause
explanation: Nesting means one IF or ELIF sits inside another IF or ELIF block. Statements written one after another are sequential, and an ELIF chain with an ELSE is a chained conditional, not a nested one.

q: In a nested structure with an outer if condition1 that contains an inner if condition2 with its own else (and an outer else), when does the inner else execute?
options: When condition1 is false, regardless of the value of condition2
When condition1 is true and condition2 is false
When condition1 and condition2 are both false at the same time
When both condition1 and condition2 evaluate to True together
explanation: The inner block is reached only when condition1 is true, and its else runs when condition2 is false. If condition1 is false, the outer else runs. Both true runs the inner if body.

q: In a nested check that prints one of three messages (positive and even, positive but odd, or not positive), using if num > 0 on the outside and num % 2 == 0 on the inside, which message prints for num = -4?
options: The number is positive and is even.
The number is positive but odd.
No message, because the inner check is never reached for negatives
The number is not positive.
explanation: -4 fails the outer test num > 0, so the outer else prints The number is not positive. The even test is never reached, even though -4 is even. Because the outer else exists, a message is always printed.

q: In the even/odd check, why is the test num % 2 == 0 used?
options: % divides num by 2 and returns the whole-number quotient, which must be 0
% raises num to the power of 2 and compares the result to 0
% returns the remainder after dividing by 2, and a remainder of 0 means even
% returns True for positive numbers, so == 0 identifies negative numbers
explanation: % is the remainder (modulo) operator. An even number divides by 2 with remainder 0. It does not give the quotient, does not raise to a power, and does not test sign.

q: In the login program, what is printed when the username is "admin" and the password entered is "letmein"?
options: Invalid password.
Invalid username.
Login successful.
Invalid username. followed by Invalid password.
explanation: The username matches, so the inner if is reached. The password does not equal admin1234password, so the inner else prints Invalid password. Only one of the three messages is ever printed.

q: In the login program, what is printed when the username is "guest" but the password is the correct "admin1234password"?
options: Login successful., because the password is correct
Invalid password., because the username check passes by default
Login successful. followed by Invalid username.
Invalid username.
explanation: The outer if checks the username first. "guest" fails it, so the outer else prints Invalid username. and the password is never examined.

q: What is a common use of nested conditionals in programs that ask for input?
options: Repeating a block of code a fixed number of times while a counter changes
Validation and authentication when a program asks for user input
Converting user-entered strings to integers before they are compared
Declaring Boolean variables and assigning them initial True values
explanation: Nested conditionals check one requirement and then another, as in a login system that checks username and then password. Repetition is done by loops, and conversion and declaration are not what nesting does.

q: Match case statements were introduced in which Python version, and what kind of structure are they?
options: Python 3.10; a value-matching decision-control structure
Python 2.7; a looping structure that repeats cases until a match is found
Python 3.0; a function-definition structure that names reusable cases
Python 3.6; an exception-handling structure that catches unmatched values
explanation: Match case arrived in Python 3.10 and is a value-matching decision-control structure. It does not loop, define functions, or handle exceptions.

q: What is a key limitation of match case statements relative to chained conditional statements?
options: It cannot compare string values, only integers can be matched
It can handle at most two possible values in one statement
It does not support relational or logical operators
It has no way of specifying a branch for unmatched values
explanation: Match case is similar to chained conditionals but does not support relational or logical operators in the case values (an if guard can add an extra condition). It matches strings and many values, and case _ provides a branch for unmatched values.

q: Which line pair shows the correct match-case syntax in Python?
options: switch <expression>: followed by case <value>:
match (<expression>) { case <value>: } with curly braces
case <expression>: followed by match <value>:
match <expression>: followed by case <value>:
explanation: Python writes match <expression>: and then indented case <value>: lines. switch is not a Python keyword here, braces are not used, and case cannot come before match.
